column2: When her husband arrived she quickly fled southward: "Who could be my protector here — the sages or the gods?"
As his beloved mare ran, the Sun himself, in the form of a horse, ran after her wherever Usha went.
Who, fallen under the sway of the planet of love, does not act unseemly? The Bhagirathi and other rivers, forests and groves,
the Narmada and the Vindhya — both running southward passed them, and the daughter of Tvashtri, distressed with fear, reached the Gautami.
There are sages at Janasthana who will protect me, she had heard; the mare entered the hermitage of the sages and the Gautami.
The Sun in the form of a horse followed her there; the sages' sons dwelling at Janasthana stopped the horse. Then the lord, husband of Usha, cursed those sages in anger:
Since you hold me back, you will become banyan trees.
Through the eye of wisdom the sages knew the horse to be Usha's husband; the sages joyfully praised that Sun, lord of the gods.
Praised by the hosts of sages, the Sun then approached the mare; his face in the form of a horse touched the mare's face.
Recognising her husband, the daughter of Tvashtri released seed from her mouth; from the seed of the two, the Ashvins were born in the Ganga.
There came the hosts of gods, the Siddhas and sages, the rivers, cows, plants, gods and hosts of luminaries,
the holy chariot with seven horses, Aruna the Sun's charioteer, Yama, Manu, Varuna and Shani, son of Vivasvan,
the holy river Yamuna and the great river Tapi; taking their respective forms, those rivers, O sage, in wonder
came to see, filled with astonishment, and the father-in-law too. Knowing his intention, the Sun said to his father-in-law:
O Tvashtri, for the pleasure of Usha, who is performing supreme austerity, mount me on the lathe and cut away my splendour many times; cut as much as will bring her comfort, O lord of creatures.
Saying "So be it," Tvashtri then cut away his splendour in the presence of Somanatha; hence they know it as Prabhasa.
Where she in the form of a mare was united with her husband in the Gautami, and where the Ashvins were born, that is called Ashvatirtha.
It is also known as Bhanutirtha and as the Panchavata hermitage; the Tapi and the Yamuna came to see their father.
The confluence of the rivers Aruna and Varuna with the Ganga is auspicious; of the holy places of the gods who came there separately,
there are twelve thousand virtuous holy places; bathing and giving there all grant imperishable merit.
By remembering, reading or hearing it, O Narada, one becomes freed from all sins, righteous and happy.

Whatever is dearest, powerful masters give to their servants; others give, but you will take away what I have brought.
brahmapuran:90:16	Look, the three-eyed god will release the serpent through Nandin; you will give Nandin the serpent I obtained.
brahmapuran:90:17	I always carry you, master; you should always give to me. It is not fitting to say 'give' about the serpent I obtained.
brahmapuran:90:18	This is not the conduct of good masters who act rightly; the good give to their servants, but you take what I have gained.
brahmapuran:90:19	You conquer the Daityas in battle only by my strength, O Keshava, yet you vainly boast, 'I am very mighty.'
Hearing these words of Garuda, the bearer of discus and mace laughed and, near Nandin, as the guardians of the worlds looked on,
the wise one said: "Carrying me you have become lean, O best of birds; by your strength I shall conquer all the Asuras."
Having said this, O Brahman, the lord of Shri, his anger calmed, said: "Carry just the little finger of my hand, near Nandin."
Then, placing it on Garuda's head, he said again: "If you truly carry me always, see what is right, O bird."
When the finger was placed, his head sank into his belly, and his belly sank between his feet, and he was crushed. Then, wretched, pained and ashamed, with joined palms:

Save me, save me, lord of the world, your offending servant; you are the lord of all worlds, the upholder and the one to be upheld.
brahmapuran:90:26	The mighty forgive thousands of offences; great is the compassion of one who shows it even to an offender.
brahmapuran:90:27	All the sages call you alone the mine of compassion. Protect me, distressed, Mother of the world who dwells in the lotus; O Kamala, protect this wretched, suffering child, you who love your children.
Then the goddess Shri, full of compassion, also said to Janardana:
Protect, Lord, your own servant Garuda who has fallen into distress. Janardana said this to Nandin, Shambhu's mount:
Take the serpent together with Garuda to Shambhu. By his grace, when Garuda is looked upon by Maheshvara, Garuda will regain his own form.
Saying "So be it," the bull went slowly with the serpent and Garuda to Shankara and told him everything. Shankara, the moon-crested, said to Garutman:

Go, mighty-armed one, to the Ganga, the Gautami, purifier of the world, granting all desires and peaceful; bathing in her, you will regain your body
brahmapuran:90:33	and obtain all desires a hundredfold and a thousandfold. For living beings tormented by all sins, whose efforts have been uprooted by ill fortune, the Gautami is the refuge that grants their wishes, O bird.
Hearing his words, bowing, Garuda went; having bathed in the Ganga, Garuda bowed to Shiva and Vishnu.
Then the bird became golden, with a body of diamond, mighty and swift, O best of sages, and the wise one returned to Vishnu.
From then on that holy place is called Garuda, granting all desires; whatever bathing and the like a disciplined man does there is all imperishable, my child, and brings the love of Shiva and Vishnu.
Having done cleansing and the rest, bathing, twilight worship and all else in due order, and having bowed to the brahmins, he then goes about his own work.
In the morning, when he goes to the Gautami, he is ugly, all his limbs loose with leprosy, oozing pus and blood;
when, having bathed in the Gautami Ganga, he returns, he bears a beautiful form, calm, like the sun and fire, like the sun embodied.
The brahmin himself never sees these two forms of his. Where the Lord Galava, devoted to austerity and knowledge,
resorting to the goddess Gautami, stays surrounded by sages, the brahmin too comes daily to that holy place,
and bowing to Galava, then goes to his own house. The body the one born of Sana had before resorting to the Ganga,
and the one he had again after bathing and the twilight worship — both forms of that brahmin Galava saw every day.
Seeing it, astonished, he thought, "There must be some reason for this." Thus astonished, Galava said to that brahmin,
when the one born of Sana bowed and was going home; the wise teacher carefully called him, with compassion and wonder:
Who are you, where will you go, what do you do, where will you eat, what is your name, where is your bed, who is your wife? Tell me.
Hearing Galava's words, the brahmin said to the sage:
Tomorrow I will tell you everything, having determined what is to be done.
Having said this to Galava, the one born of Sana went home; having eaten at night and gone properly to bed with the courtesan, remembering Galava's words, he said, startled:

You are endowed with every virtue; though a courtesan, you are faithful. May our mutual love continue as long as we live.
brahmapuran:92:29	Yet I ask you something: what is your name, what is your family, what is your place, who are your kin? Tell me everything.

There was a pure, consecrated brahmin known as Dhritavrata; I am his wife Mahi, and my son was left in Galava's hermitage,
brahmapuran:92:31	an intelligent boy known as the one born of Sana. Through a former fault I abandoned the dharma of my family and live here as a wanton woman; know me to be a brahmin woman, O brahmin.
Hearing her words, he was as if pierced in a vital spot and suddenly fell to the ground; the courtesan said to him:
What has happened, best of brahmins? Where has your love gone? What have I said that has troubled your heart?
Composing himself, the brahmin said:
My father was the brahmin Dhritavrata; I am his son, born of Sana; my mother is Mahi — she has come to me by fate.
Hearing his words, she too became deeply grieved. After they had grieved, at clear dawn the brahmin went to Galava, tiger among sages, and told him:

O Brahman, I am the son of Dhritavrata, formerly raised by you and invested with the sacred thread by you; Mahi is my mother, O Lord.
brahmapuran:92:38	What shall I do, and by doing what would there be expiation for me?
Hearing the brahmin's words, Galava said, "Do not grieve. I see this twofold form of yours daily, as never before.
That is why I asked you the story; I have heard and understood it. Whatever you did has been destroyed in the Ganga.
By the greatness of this holy place and the grace of this goddess you are purified daily, my child; there is no need to deliberate.
In the morning I see your forms sinful day and night, and again I see your form excellent in virtue.
I always see you coming burdened with sin and going sinless; therefore you have now been purified by the goddess.
So nothing remains for you to do. And this is your mother, O brahmin, known to be a courtesan;
she has repented greatly and turned away from sin. Attachment to sense-objects is natural to beings, my child;
through the company of the good and great merit, turning away comes by divine grace. She has repented exceedingly through merit done before.
Bathing at this holy place she will then be purified." And so, O Narada, mother and son both did so,
and by bathing both became free of sin, without doubt. From then on that holy place is called Dhautapapa,
famed as Papapranashana and Galava. Great sin, small sin, or minor sin — this Dhautapapa destroys all, granting great merit.
Seeing that deed, the disciples reported the hawk to the sage: "The pot has been stolen, best of sages, by the foolish hawk."
Then the Lord became angry and wished to curse Hari; knowing it, the lord of the gods made the pot full of honey
and the bird Hari put it back on the embers. Seeing the pot filled with honey, Vishvamitra became angry; looking at the pot, Kaushika said in anger:
Give us only the dog's meat; you take away the excellent nectar. Otherwise I will reduce you to ashes. Indra, afraid, then said:
Having offered the honey properly, drink it with your sons; what use is this impure dog's meat, great sage?
Vishvamitra said "No: what fruit is there in one person eating? All the people are suffering; what use is that honey, O Hari?
If there is nectar for all, I will eat pure nectar; otherwise, when the gods and ancestors have eaten this dog's meat,
then I will eat that meat afterwards; I have no falsehood." Then the thousand-eyed one, afraid, at once summoned the clouds,
and rained nectar-water, and the people were given nectar. Afterwards that holy nectar given by Hari, according to rule,
having first satisfied the gods and satisfied the three worlds, the brahmin Vishvamitra ate with his disciples and his wife.
From then on that holy place has been famed as giving very great merit, where the lord of gods came and nectar was given to the worlds,
and it became free of meat; that holy place gives merit to men; bathing and giving there grant the fruit of all sacrifices.
From then on that holy place is remembered as Vishvamitra, as Madhutirtha, as Aindra, Shyena and Parjanya.
Fever, the threefold sin and the hells, each separately, make haste! Having said this to them, Yama went quickly,
surrounded by these and others, to where the best of brahmins Shveta was. Seeing Yama coming, the armed Nandin spoke
to Vinayaka, Skanda and Dandin, lord of beings; there a battle arose there, terrifying to all worlds.
Karttikeya himself pierced Yama's servants with his spear, and struck down the mighty lord of the southern quarter.
The surviving servants of Yama told the Sun; the Sun too, with the gods, hearing that great wonder,
followed by the guardians of the worlds, came to me. I, the Lord Vishnu, Indra, Agni and Varuna,
the moon and sun, the Ashvins, the guardians of the worlds and the hosts of Maruts — these and many others, we went to Yama.
The mighty lord of the south lay dead on the bank of the Ganga. The oceans, rivers, Nagas and many various beings
came there to see Yama, son of Vivasvan, lord of the gods. Seeing Yama with his army slain, the gods, stricken with fear, all spoke to Shambhu again and again with joined palms:

Love for devotion is ever yours, and the slaying of the wicked. O primal maker, salutation to you; O blue-throated one, salutation to you; beloved of Brahma, salutation to you; beloved of the gods, salutation to you.
brahmapuran:94:28	To take the brahmin Shveta, your devotee, whose life had ended, Yama and all the rest were unable; seeing this we are supremely content: your love for devotees is true, O Lord.
brahmapuran:94:29	Those who have taken refuge in you, the compassionate, even Death cannot look upon; knowing this, all worship you alone, Shiva, with supreme devotion.
brahmapuran:94:30	You alone are lord of the worlds; do you not remember, Shankara? Without you, who is able here to maintain order, O Lord?
As they praised thus, Shiva appeared before them and said, "What shall I give?" and the gods said this:

This son of Vivasvan is Dharma, the restrainer of all embodied beings, established as guardian of the worlds in ordering dharma and adharma.
brahmapuran:94:33	He does not deserve death; he is neither offender nor sinner; without him nothing of the world's sustainer will be accomplished.
brahmapuran:94:34	Therefore, O lord of gods, revive Yama with his army and mounts; a prayer to the great, O Lord, should not be in vain.
Then the Lord said, "I will revive Yama without doubt, if the gods today agree to my word."
Then all the gods said, "We will do what you say — you under whose control is the whole world with Hari, Brahma and the rest."
Then the Lord said to the assembled immortals, "Let my devotee not go to death." The immortals said again, "No:
then all worlds, moving and unmoving, would be immortal, O god; this distinction of mortal and immortal would not exist, O god who are the world."
Again Shambhu said to them, "Hear my words: of my devotees and Vishnu's devotees who serve the Gautami,
we are always the masters; Death does not deserve mastery; Yama should never even speak of them.
They should never be overcome by mental and bodily afflictions; those who take refuge in Shiva are freed at that very moment.
Therefore all of them are to be saluted by Yama and his followers." The hosts of gods said "So be it" to Shiva, god of gods.
Then the Lord, the master, said to Nandin, his mount:
Sprinkle the dead Yama with the water of the Gautami.
Then Yama and all the others, sprinkled by Nandin, rose up alive and went to the southern quarter.
On the northern bank of the Gautami all the deities led by Vishnu remained, worshipping the god of gods Maheshvara.
There were eighty thousand and fourteen thousand, and likewise six thousand and again six thousand,
and six on the southern bank, thirty thousand holy places. This is the holy account of Shvetatirtha, O Narada.
Where Death fell, that is called Mrityutirtha; by merely hearing of it one lives a thousand years.
Bathing and giving there destroy all sins; hearing, reading and remembering it destroy impurity and grant enjoyment and liberation to all worlds.
Kavi, noble-minded, with joined palms, also said to the lord of gods:
The knowledge that is beyond the reach even of Brahma and the sages — that knowledge I ask, O Lord; you are my teacher and my god.
The knowledge that revives the dead, unknown even to the gods, the best of gods gave to Shukra who asked for it.
Other knowledge, worldly or Vedic, is within others' reach; when Shankara is pleased, what more remains to consider?
Having obtained the great knowledge, he went to his father and teacher; and Kavi, honoured for his knowledge, became the teacher of the Daityas.
Then once, for some other reason, Kacha, son of Brihaspati, obtained that knowledge from Kavi;
from Kacha Brihaspati, and then the gods one by one, obtained the great knowledge called the reviver of the dead.
Where Kavi obtained it by worshipping Maheshvara, on the northern bank of the Gautami, that is called Shukratirtha,
the holy place of the reviver of the dead, increasing life and health; whatever bathing and giving is done there grants imperishable merit.
Then a battle arose as between gods and Danavas; having conquered in battle his elder brother, the peaceful lord of wealth,
he took away the Pushpaka, the city of Lanka and everything. Ravana proclaimed in the three worlds with all that moves and does not move:
Whoever gives shelter to my brother shall be slain by me. Driven out by his brother, Vaishravana found shelter nowhere; going to his grandfather Pulastya and bowing, he said:
Driven out by my wicked brother, what shall I do? Tell me what shelter or refuge there may be — a deity or a holy place.
Hearing his grandson's words, Pulastya said:

Go to the Gautami, my son, and praise the god Maheshvara; he cannot enter there, into the midst of the Ganga's waters.
brahmapuran:97:17	You will attain auspicious success; do so with me.
Saying "So be it," the lord of wealth went with his wife, with his father, mother and the aged Pulastya.
Going to the Gautami Ganga, pure, bathing and keeping his vow, he praised Shiva, lord of the god of gods, giver of enjoyment and liberation:

You alone are the master of this moving and unmoving universe, O Shambhu; there is none higher. Whoever here out of delusion scorns you and acts boldly is only to be pitied.
brahmapuran:97:21	With your eightfold form you uphold all; everything proceeds by your command; yet the wise know you, never the ignorant — ancient is your greatness.
brahmapuran:97:22	The mother playfully said, 'This brave one born of dirt is your son, O god'; and by your glance he became the king of obstacles — ah, the working of the Lord's gaze!
brahmapuran:97:23	Girija, her limbs wet with tears, seeing the couple separated, said so to the Lord; and the mind-born one became Madana, and Rati regained her former good fortune from Soma.
As he praised thus, the three-eyed god appeared before him and offered a boon; out of joy he said nothing.
When the lord of wealth and Pulastya were silent, and Shiva, delighted, kept saying again and again "Choose a boon,"
meanwhile a bodiless voice spoke there, saying this to Maheshvara: "Guardianship of wealth is to be obtained."
As if knowing the mind of Pulastya and of Vaishravana's father, the voice then uttered an auspicious meaning.
What is to be is as though it were; what is to be given is as though given; what is to be obtained is as though obtained — such was the auspicious divine voice there:
He who had powerful enemies and was overcome by sorrow, having worshipped the linga of Someshvara, obtained lordship of a quarter, mastery of wealth, boundless generosity, wife and sons.
Hearing that voice, the lord of wealth said to the trident-bearing god of gods, "Let it be so."
So be it, the lord of gods approved the divine voice; and with holy boons he gladdened Pulastya and the sage Vishravas
and the guardian of wealth, and Shiva, lord of gods, departed. From then on that holy place is known as Paulastya and Dhanada,
and as the holy Vaishravasa, auspicious and granting all desires; whatever bathing and the like is done there grants much merit.

That too would be mine, O gods; I am not able to accomplish the task, though the task of Jataveda is yours in every way.
brahmapuran:98:12	Having come into this state, I do not know how it will be for me; there may be no power in me to pervade here and hereafter.
brahmapuran:98:13	Yet when the task is being done, that will be my course. The gods and sages spoke to him with all their feeling:

Long life, delight in action and power of pervasion are given; we shall give you the Prayaja and Anuyaja offerings, O bearer of oblations.
brahmapuran:98:15	You are the best mouth of the gods; the first oblations are yours; what substance you give, we shall eat, O best of gods.
Then fire was pleased by the words of the gods in order; here and hereafter in pervasion, in oblation and in worldly use,
everywhere fire became fearless and capable by the gods' command — Jataveda, Brihadbhanu, seven-flamed, blue-red,
he is called water-born, shami-born and sacrifice-born. Drawing him out of the water, the gods consecrated fire;
fire came to dwell in both places, all-pervading. The gods went as they had come; that is called Vahnitirtha.
There were seven hundred virtuous holy places there; whoever, self-controlled, bathes and gives at them
obtains the full, auspicious fruit of a horse sacrifice and more. There too is Devatirtha, Agneya and Jatavedasa;
there stands a linga installed by Agni, of many colours; merely by seeing that god one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
Hearing it, filled with wonder, he thought, "What shall I do?" He told the sages known as the Valakhilyas.
They said to the brahmin Kashyapa, "Go to the Ganga, the Gautami, and praise Maheshvara there; your wives will be restored,
where the god Maheshvara, out of fear of brahmin-slaying, always dwells in the midst of the Ganga under the name Madhyameshvara."
Saying "So be it," Kashyapa, bathing in the Ganga and keeping his vow, praised the god of gods Maheshvara with holy praises:

May he who is sole lord of the three worlds and has not the slightest pride in anything, the lord of the perfected, maker of the whole universe, husband of Shiva, be gracious.
brahmapuran:100:20	For embodied beings, unmoving and moving, scorched by the heat of the threefold suffering and running here and there, you alone are skilled in removing sorrow.
brahmapuran:100:21	Whose threefold union with sattva and the others even Shakra and the rest cannot describe — reflecting on Soma's wondrous conduct, one is ever happy; he is ever generous and adorable.
Praised with such hymns, the god Shiva, husband of Gauri, being pleased, Shambhu gave Kashyapa many boons.
To him who sought his wives he said: "Both your wives, who are in the form of rivers, on reaching the Ganga, best of rivers,
by merely meeting her will regain their own bodies." By the grace of the Ganga they became pregnant again.
Then the great-minded Prajapati, pleased at obtaining his wives, summoned the brahmins dwelling on the bank of the Gautami.
Pleased, Prajapati performed the parting-of-the-hair rite for them, and honoured the brahmins by the prescribed rite.
When the brahmins had eaten in Kashyapa's house, Kadru, seated near her husband, looking at the brahmins,
laughed at the sages with her eye, and they were angered: "Wicked one, since you laughed with your eye, let your eye be broken, sinner."
Kadru then became one-eyed — she who is called the mother of serpents. Then the Lord Kashyapa appeased the sages.
Then, pleased, they said, "The Gautami, best of rivers, will protect from thousands of offences through resort to her."
Kashyapa, best of sages, did so with his wives. From then on that holy place is known as the confluence of the two, allaying all sins and granting the fruit of all sacrifices.
Onefold, tenfold, a hundredfold and a thousandfold, O king, there is a proper answer; yet this is said:

For the sonless there is no higher world, O best of kings. The father who bathes when a son is born, O lord of people,
brahmapuran:104:8	obtains the fruit of the consecration bath of ten horse sacrifices; one's standing comes from a son, and one becomes excellent among immortals.
brahmapuran:104:9	The gods are immortal through nectar, brahmins and others through a son; a son frees his father and grandfathers from the three debts.
brahmapuran:104:10	What use is the root, what use water, what use beards, what use austerity? Without a son, O king of kings — heaven and liberation are remembered as coming from a son.
brahmapuran:104:11	A son is the highest world, dharma, desire and wealth; a son is liberation, the supreme light, the saviour of all embodied beings.
brahmapuran:104:12	Without a son, O king of kings, heaven and liberation are very hard to attain; a son alone is supreme in the world for accomplishing dharma, desire and wealth.
brahmapuran:104:13	What is given without a son, what is offered without a son, a birth without a son — it seems to me in vain.
brahmapuran:104:14	Therefore in the three worlds nothing is as desirable as a son. Hearing that, the king, filled with wonder, spoke to the two again:
Tell me truly how I may have a son, wherever it may be — by whatever means, having made some effort, by mantra, sacrifice or gifts, this son is to be begotten by me.
The two, having meditated a moment, said to Harishchandra, best of kings, who sought a son: "Go to the Gautami, O giver of honour.
There the lord of waters grants the best wish of the mind; Varuna is declared by the sages to be the giver of all.
Pleased, he will in time give you a son." Hearing this, the best of kings followed the sages' words.
Resorting to the bank of the Gautami, he pleased Varuna; then Varuna, pleased, said to Harishchandra:
I will give you a son, O king, an ornament of the three worlds, if you will sacrifice with him; then you will surely have a son.
Harishchandra said to Varuna, "I will sacrifice with him." Then Harishchandra went and made the offering-rice for Varuna,
and the king gave it to his wife; then a son was born to the king. When the son was born, the lord of waters, best of speakers, said:
Your son is to be sacrificed today; do you remember your promise?
Harishchandra said this to Varuna, according to custom:
An animal becomes fit for sacrifice after ten days; then I will sacrifice.
Hearing the king's words, Varuna went to his abode; after ten days he came again and said to the king, "Sacrifice."
The king said to Varuna, "An animal without teeth is worthless; when the animal's teeth have come, come then; go now, lord of waters."
Hearing the king's words, the lord of waters went again; when the teeth had come, at seven years, O Narada,
he said again to the king, "Sacrifice." Then the king said to Varuna, "These will fall out, lord of waters,
and others will come; then I will sacrifice; go now." Varuna went again; when the second teeth came, O Narada, he said to the king, "Sacrifice"; the king said to the lord of waters:
When a kshatriya is the victim in a sacrifice, lord of waters, when he knows the science of arms, then he is an excellent victim.
Hearing the king's words, Varuna went to his abode. When Rohita became capable in missiles and weapons,
and that subduer of foes became learned in all the Vedas and scriptures, when Rohita at sixteen had attained the rank of crown prince,
he came, pleased, to where the king was with Rohita; Varuna came and said, "Sacrifice your own son today."
Saying "Om," the best of kings spoke to the priests and to Rohita, his eldest son, while Varuna listened:
Come, my son, great hero; I will sacrifice you to Varuna.
What is this? Rohita asked his father; his father told him in detail all that had happened. Rohita said to his father, while Varuna listened:
Great king, I will first, pure and quickly, with the priests and the family priest, sacrifice to Vishnu, lord of the worlds, with an animal, and then to Varuna; please permit this.
Hearing Rohita's words, the lord of waters, filled with great anger, then afflicted King Harishchandra with dropsy.
Rohita went to the forest, taking his divine bow, mounted on his chariot, free from distress.
Where King Harishchandra had worshipped Varuna and obtained a son at the Ganga, there Rohita too went.
Five years passed, and in the sixth, staying there, the prince heard of the king's illness.
What use is it that I was born a son who causes suffering to my father? What should I do? — thus he reflected.
On its bank the prince saw holy sages; he saw a best of sages living on the bank of the Ganga,
known as Ajigarta, son of the sage Vayas, surrounded by three sons and his wife, his livelihood exhausted. Seeing him, the prince bowed and said:
Why do you appear with your livelihood exhausted, lean and as if dejected?
And Ajigarta said to Rohita, the prince:
There is no means of sustaining the body, and I have many to feed; without food we shall die. Tell me, what shall we do?
Hearing that, the prince spoke again to the sage:
What is in your mind? Tell me that, best of speakers.

I have no gold, silver, cows, grain, clothes or the like, O tiger among kings; so I have no livelihood.
brahmapuran:104:52	I have sons and a wife, and I am the fifth; will you buy any of them with food, best of kings?
What do you sell, wise Ajigarta? Tell me the truth and say nothing else; brahmins speak the truth.
Buy one of my three sons, or me, or my wife, and we will live.
What use is your wife, wise one, or you in your old age? Give me a young son, whichever of your sons you wish.
I will not sell my eldest son Shunahpuchchha, Rohita, and the mother will not sell the youngest; of these, I will sell the middle one, Shunahshepa; name the price.
A victim is to be offered to Varuna, a man of greater virtue; if you sell, tell the true price, great sage.
Saying "So be it," Ajigarta fixed the price of his son: "A thousand cows, and grain, coins and garments; O prince, give me that and I will give you my son."
Saying "So be it," Rohita gave the wealth with garments; having given it, Rohita went to his father with the sage's son and told his father of the sage's son bought by purchase:
Sacrifice to Varuna with this victim, and be free of disease.
Harishchandra spoke thus after his son's words:

Brahmins, kshatriyas and vaishyas are to be protected by the king — so says the scripture; and especially the best of brahmins are the teachers of the classes.
brahmapuran:104:63	Those who are worthy of worship even by Vishnu — how much more by one like me! By slighting whom the family of kings is destroyed —
brahmapuran:104:64	how can I, making them victims, dare to protect my own wretched self? That I should make a brahmin a victim is not proper.
brahmapuran:104:65	Better to die than ever make a brahmin a victim; therefore, my son, go happily with the brahmin.
Meanwhile a bodiless voice spoke there:

Go to the Gautami, O king of kings, with the priests and the family priest, with the brahmin's son as victim and with your son Rohita;
brahmapuran:104:68	you must perform the rite, and without the killing of Shunahshepa the rite will be completed there; therefore go, O wise one.
Hearing those words, the best of kings quickly went to the Ganga, with the sage Vishvamitra and the family priest Vasishtha,
with the sage Vamadeva and other sages; reaching that Gautami Ganga, he was consecrated for the human sacrifice.
He made the altar, pavilion, fire-pits and the rest, the sacrificial post, the victim and so on; having done everything properly, when the sacrifice began,
seeing Shunahshepa, the victim, tied to the post with mantras and sprinkled with water, Vishvamitra said this:

Let the gods, the sages, Harishchandra and especially Rohita, all give leave concerning this Shunahshepa, best of brahmins.
brahmapuran:104:74	The gods to whom this oblation is to be given, each separately — let them all especially give leave concerning Shunahshepa.
brahmapuran:104:75	With fat, hair, skins and flesh consecrated with good mantras in the sacrifice, this victim, Shunahshepa, best of brahmins, is to be offered in the fire.
brahmapuran:104:76	Let all the best of brahmins be honoured and agree with me; let the best of brahmins go to the Gautami and, having bathed, praise the gods separately
brahmapuran:104:77	with mantras and hymns and rejoice, devoted to Shiva; let the sages and the gods who eat the oblation protect him.
The sages said "So be it," and the best of kings agreed. Then Shunahshepa went to the Ganga, purifier of the three worlds,
bathed and praised the gods who eat the oblations there. Then the hosts of gods were pleased with Shunahshepa, O sage, and all the gods said, while Vishvamitra listened:
Let this rite be complete without the killing of Shunahshepa.
And especially Varuna spoke to the best of kings; then the king's human sacrifice, famed in the world, was completed.
By the grace of the gods, the grace of the sages and the grace of the holy place, the king's rite was completed.
Vishvamitra honoured Shunahshepa in the assembly and, having honoured him in the presence of the gods, made him his own son.
Kaushika made him the eldest of his sons; those sons of the wise Vishvamitra who did not accept
Shunahshepa's seniority Kaushika cursed; the sons who accepted his seniority he honoured
with a boon, O tiger among sages — this I have told you. All this happened on the southern bank of the Gautami.
There are holy places there famed among the gods and others, many of them; hear their names from me, O wise one:
Harishchandra, Shunahshepa, Vishvamitra and Rohita — such holy places number eight thousand and fourteen.
Bathing and giving at them grant the fruit of a human sacrifice. The greatness of this holy place has been told, O best of sages;
whoever reads it, causes it to be read or hears it with devotion — the sonless obtains a son, and whatever else the mind holds dear.
Then arose the excellent river Pravara, auspicious and nectar-like, born of Rahu's body and endowed with the power of Rudra.
The delightful Amrita, best of rivers, was sent forth then; there are five thousand virtuous holy places there.
There Shambhu himself always stood, worshipped by the gods; all the gods, pleased with that goddess river, each separately
joyfully gave boons: "As Shambhu, lord of the gods, receives worship in the world, so you will receive worship.
Dwell, O goddess, for the good of the worlds; always stay, queen of waters, granting all perfections to all.
By praise, recitation and meditation you grant all desires; those who always bow to you with devotion, hoping for something,
all their tasks will be fulfilled by the command of the gods." Since the dwelling of Shiva and Shakti was eternal there,
therefore the sages call it Nivasapura. Long ago the gods, well pleased, gave boons to the Pravara:

Your confluence with the Ganga will be famed and dear to the gods; for all who bathe there there will be enjoyment or liberation,
brahmapuran:106:56	or whatever the mind desires, even what is rare for the gods — all will be theirs here. Having given this, the gods went.
From then on that holy place is known as the confluence of the Pravara. The power that was sent forth by the god of gods
is famed as Amrita, and thus the great river Pravara.
Having said this to Gautama, the old woman prayed to Fire and made that sage learned and handsome.
Then, learned, fortunate and lovely, he, full of affection, made the old woman his wife, and joyful at heart he delighted with that charming one in the cave for many years.
Once, while the couple were living joyfully in the cave on the mountain, O tiger among sages, spotless sages came there,
Vasishtha, Vamadeva and other great sages; wandering through holy places they reached his cave.
Knowing the sages had come, Gautama with his wife showed them hospitality; some of them laughed at him.
Those who were young, intoxicated with youth, and those of middle age, seeing the old woman and Gautama, some laughed there:
Is this your son or grandson, old woman? Who has become Gautama? Tell the truth, auspicious one — so the brahmins laughed.
A young woman is poison to an old man; a young man is nectar to an old woman. Ah, after a long time we have seen a union of the desired and the undesired!
So some said as the couple listened; having said this and received hospitality, all the great sages left.
Hearing the sages' words, both were deeply grieved and ashamed; the very wise Gautama with his wife asked Agastya, tiger among sages, best of seers:
What land or holy place is there where good is quickly attained, O very wise one, granting enjoyment and liberation?

O Brahman, I have heard these words from sages speaking: all desires are fulfilled there at the Gautami, without doubt.
brahmapuran:107:52	Therefore go, O wise one, to the Gautami, destroyer of sin; I will follow you; do as you wish.
Hearing Agastya's words, Gautama went with the old woman; there the Lord sage performed fierce austerity with his wife.
The Lord sage praised the god Shambhu and likewise Vishnu, and propitiated the Ganga for his wife's sake:

For the weary in this existence you alone are the auspicious refuge, like a tree with its shade for travellers in the desert.
brahmapuran:107:56	In every way you remove the sins of beings high and low, as a cloud does for crops withering in drought, O dark one.
brahmapuran:107:57	You are the ladder to the fortress of Vaikuntha, a river of nectar; be the refuge, O Gautami, of those who have fallen and are tormented.
